# Buffers

**Package** `buffers.v1`

## Messages

### `ServiceOptions`

ServiceOptions shapes how one service lands in each target.

| Field | Type | # | Behavior | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `skip` | `bool` | 1 |  | skip excludes the service from every target. |
| `capnp_id` | `int64` | 3 |  | capnp_interface controls whether a Cap'n Proto `interface` is emitted. Optional rather than a bare bool because the default is not a constant: a service with methods becomes an interface, and one with none does not. A bare bool would make "false" and "unset" indistinguishable, so a service could not opt out. capnp_id pins the interface's Cap'n Proto ID. Derived from the file ID and the service's fully qualified name when unset. See buffers.v1.FileOptions.capnp_id on why a valid ID reads as negative. |
| `targets` | `repeated string` | 5 |  | ros_service controls whether .srv files are emitted for the service's methods. Defaults to true for a service whose methods classify as AIP standard methods, since those have a request and response shape ROS can express, and false otherwise. targets restricts the service to the named targets. See buffers.v1.MessageOptions.targets. |

### `MethodOptions`

MethodOptions shapes how one method lands in each target.

| Field | Type | # | Behavior | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `skip` | `bool` | 1 |  | skip excludes the method. It permanently consumes its Cap'n Proto ordinal, for the same reason buffers.v1.FieldOptions.skip does. |
| `ordinal` | `int32` | 2 |  | ordinal pins the Cap'n Proto method ordinal, 0-based within the interface. Leave it unset. Derivation orders methods by declaration order and records the result in buffers.lock, so a method inserted in the middle of a service is caught as drift rather than silently renumbering every method after it. |
| `transport` | `Transport` | 3 |  | transport selects the call shape. See Transport. |
| `topic` | `string` | 4 |  | topic overrides the ROS topic name for a TRANSPORT_TOPIC method, which otherwise derives from the method name in snake_case. It is also the name an eCAL publisher and subscriber pair will be generated against. |
| `ros_type` | `string` | 5 |  | ros_type overrides the emitted .srv or .action base name, which is otherwise the method name. |
| `targets` | `repeated string` | 6 |  | targets restricts the method to the named targets. See buffers.v1.MessageOptions.targets. |

### `FileOptions`

FileOptions carries the per-file names each target needs and proto does not declare.  Applied via:  option (buffers.v1.file) = { namespace: "sensors.v1" ros_package: "sensor_msgs" file_id: "SNSR" };

| Field | Type | # | Behavior | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `namespace` | `string` | 1 |  | namespace is the FlatBuffers `namespace` and the Cap'n Proto `$Cxx.namespace`. Defaults to the proto package, which is already dotted. |
| `capnp_id` | `int64` | 2 |  | capnp_id pins the file's Cap'n Proto 64-bit ID. Left unset, the plugin derives one deterministically from the proto file path (see protokit's buffers/capnpid.go) so that regenerating a schema produces the same ID rather than the random one `capnp id` would mint. Set it when adopting a .capnp file that already exists in the wild: its ID is part of every consumer's build, and rederiving it would orphan them. Cap'n Proto requires the high bit set, so every valid ID read as a signed integer is negative. That is the identity's bit pattern, not a quantity, and the plugin renders it as `@0x%016x` of the same 64 bits. |
| `ros_package` | `string` | 3 |  | ros_package is the ROS 2 package the emitted .msg and .srv files belong to. Defaults to the proto package's first segment with dots replaced by underscores, which is the ROS naming rule. |
| `jvm_package` | `string` | 4 |  | jvm_package is the Kotlin or Java package Square Wire generates into. Defaults to the file's `java_package` when it declares one, then to the proto package. |
| `file_id` | `string` | 5 |  | file_id is the FlatBuffers `file_identifier`: a 4-character magic string stamped into the buffer so a reader can reject a payload that is not the schema it expected. Exactly 4 ASCII characters, or empty for none. |
| `file_extension` | `string` | 6 |  | file_extension is the FlatBuffers `file_extension` used for binary payloads written by the generated code, for example "bin". |
| `fbs_include` | `repeated string` | 7 |  | fbs_include adds `include` lines to the emitted .fbs beyond the ones derived from the proto's own imports. An escape hatch for hand-written schema that the generated file must compose with. |

### `MessageOptions`

MessageOptions shapes how one message lands in each target.

| Field | Type | # | Behavior | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `skip` | `bool` | 1 |  | skip excludes the message from every target. A message reachable only from a skipped message is not itself skipped: reachability is not a policy, and silently dropping a type someone else imports is worse than emitting an unused one. |
| `layout` | `Layout` | 2 |  | layout selects the FlatBuffers table or struct distinction. See Layout. |
| `capnp_id` | `int64` | 3 |  | capnp_id pins this type's Cap'n Proto ID, for the same adoption reason FileOptions.capnp_id exists. Derived from the file ID and the type's fully qualified name when unset. |
| `targets` | `repeated string` | 4 |  | targets restricts the message to the named targets: "flatbuffers", "capnp", "ros", or "wire". Empty means every target, which is the norm; a non-empty list is how a message that only makes sense over one wire — a ROS-only diagnostic record, say — stays out of the others. |
| `ros_type` | `string` | 5 |  | ros_type overrides the ROS type name, which is otherwise the proto message name. ROS requires one message per file named after the type, so this renames the emitted file too. |
| `fbs_original_order` | `bool` | 6 |  | fbs_original_order emits FlatBuffers' `(original_order)` attribute, which stops flatc reordering a table's fields by size for packing. It is rarely needed here, because this plugin assigns every field an explicit `id:` and explicit ids already fix the vtable slots. It matters when the emitted schema is hand-edited afterwards to drop those ids. |
| `fbs_root` | `bool` | 7 |  | fbs_root marks this message as the emitted .fbs file's `root_type`. FlatBuffers allows one root per schema file, and it is what `GetRootAsX` is generated for. Nothing in a .proto identifies it: a file typically holds several messages and proto has no notion of which one is the payload rather than a part of it, so it has to be said here. Setting `file_id` without marking a root is a diagnostic, because a FlatBuffers `file_identifier` is only legal alongside a `root_type` — flatc rejects the pair, and finding that out from flatc rather than from here costs a round trip through a toolchain the plugin may not have run. At most one message per file may set it. |

### `FieldOptions`

FieldOptions shapes how one field lands in each target.

| Field | Type | # | Behavior | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `skip` | `bool` | 1 |  | skip excludes the field from every target. On a serialization schema this is a sharper instrument than it looks: a skipped field is not merely absent from the generated code, it permanently consumes its ordinal, because a later run that unskips it must land on the same slot. The plugin records skipped fields in buffers.lock for that reason. |
| `ordinal` | `int32` | 2 |  | ordinal pins the field's target slot: the FlatBuffers `id:` attribute and the Cap'n Proto `@N`. Leave it unset. The plugin derives a stable ordinal from the proto field number (see protokit's buffers/ordinal.go), and a derived ordinal that never moves is worth more than a hand-written one that can be typo'd into aliasing another field. Set it only to adopt an existing .capnp or .fbs whose slots were assigned before this plugin existed — which is precisely the case the derivation cannot reconstruct. Ordinals are 0-based, matching both target formats and unlike proto field numbers, which start at 1. |
| `key` | `bool` | 3 |  | key marks the field as the FlatBuffers `(key)`: the one field a vector of this table may be sorted by and binary-searched on. At most one per table. |
| `shared` | `bool` | 4 |  | shared emits FlatBuffers' `(shared)` on a string field, so identical values are written once and referenced twice. Worth it for a repeated enum-like string; wasted on a field whose values are all distinct. |
| `max_len` | `int32` | 5 |  | max_len bounds a repeated field or string for ROS, emitting `T[<=N]` or `string<=N`. ROS bounds are part of the type, and an unbounded sequence in a real-time message is the kind of thing a reviewer is looking for. Ignored by targets whose types carry no bound. |
| `fixed_len` | `int32` | 6 |  | fixed_len makes a repeated field a ROS fixed-size array, `T[N]`, and a FlatBuffers fixed-size array inside a struct. The proto side stays `repeated`, because proto cannot express a length. That makes this a claim the producer must uphold rather than one the schema enforces, and the generated doc comment says so on every affected field. |
| `ros_default` | `string` | 7 |  | ros_default is a literal default value for the ROS field, emitted after the field name. ROS defaults are a message-definition feature with no proto equivalent, since proto3 has no field defaults. |
| `capnp_group` | `string` | 8 |  | capnp_group folds this field, with every other field naming the same group, into a Cap'n Proto `group`. Groups cost nothing on the wire — they are presentation over the same slots — and are how a flat proto message with an obvious internal grouping reads well in Cap'n Proto without changing layout. |
| `targets` | `repeated string` | 9 |  | targets restricts the field to the named targets. See buffers.v1.MessageOptions.targets. |

### `EnumOptions`

EnumOptions shapes how one enum lands in each target.

| Field | Type | # | Behavior | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `skip` | `bool` | 1 |  | skip excludes the enum from every target. |
| `underlying` | `IntWidth` | 2 |  | underlying is the FlatBuffers enum's underlying integer type. Defaults to INT_WIDTH_INT32, matching proto's own encoding; narrow it where the values fit and the density matters. The plugin rejects a width that cannot hold every declared value, rather than truncating. |
| `bit_flags` | `bool` | 3 |  | bit_flags emits FlatBuffers' `(bit_flags)`, turning the enum into a bitmask whose declared values are bit positions rather than values. AIP-126 requires a zero `_UNSPECIFIED` value, and a bit_flags enum cannot have one — position 0 is a real bit. The plugin drops the unspecified value for this enum only, and says so in a diagnostic, because silently keeping it would make bit 0 mean "unspecified" for every consumer. |

## Enums

### `Transport`

Transport names how a method's messages move, where the target distinguishes between a call and a stream.  ROS is the target that cares: a request and response pair is a service, a fire-and-forget stream is a topic, and a long-running call with feedback is an action. Cap'n Proto reads it too, to decide whether a method returns a value or a stream capability.

| Value | # | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TRANSPORT_UNSPECIFIED` | 0 | TRANSPORT_UNSPECIFIED lets the plugin classify from the method's own shape: a server-streaming method becomes a topic, an AIP-151 long-running method becomes an action, and everything else becomes a call. |
| `TRANSPORT_CALL` | 1 | TRANSPORT_CALL is a request and response pair — a ROS service, a Cap'n Proto method returning results. |
| `TRANSPORT_TOPIC` | 2 | TRANSPORT_TOPIC is a one-way publication. The method's output message is the topic payload; its input is ignored, and the plugin warns when that input is not the empty message, because a topic has nowhere to put it. |
| `TRANSPORT_ACTION` | 3 | TRANSPORT_ACTION is a goal, feedback and result triple — a ROS action. The method must be AIP-151 long-running, returning google.longrunning.Operation, for the three payloads to be derivable; the plugin errors naming the method otherwise. |

### `Layout`

Layout selects how a message is laid out in a target that distinguishes between an evolvable record and a packed one.  It matters in exactly one target today — FlatBuffers, where a `table` carries a vtable and tolerates added and removed fields, while a `struct` is a fixed-size inline blob with no vtable, no defaults, and no evolution. The distinction is the difference between a 40-byte pose that memcpy's out of a shared-memory segment and one that costs a vtable indirection per field, which is why a robotics payload cares.  It is declared here rather than in a FlatBuffers-specific option because the same statement — this record is fixed-shape and I am trading evolution for density — is the one Cap'n Proto reads to decide a field belongs in the data section rather than the pointer section.

| Value | # | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LAYOUT_UNSPECIFIED` | 0 | LAYOUT_UNSPECIFIED means LAYOUT_TABLE. The default is not inferred from the message's shape, and deliberately so. A message of three doubles is struct-eligible; adding a string to it is an ordinary, wire-compatible proto change. If the layout were inferred, that edit would silently flip the message from a packed struct to a vtable-backed table — which *is* a breaking change in FlatBuffers — and nothing would say so. Packing is a deliberate trade of evolution for density, so it is opted into rather than fallen into. |
| `LAYOUT_TABLE` | 1 | LAYOUT_TABLE is the evolvable, vtable-backed record. Always legal. |
| `LAYOUT_STRUCT` | 2 | LAYOUT_STRUCT is the packed, fixed-size record. A message is only eligible when every field is a fixed-width scalar, an enum, or another struct: no strings, no bytes, no repeated fields, no maps, no oneofs, and no message fields that are themselves tables. Asking for it on a message that does not qualify is a build error naming the field that disqualified it, rather than a silent downgrade — because the caller chose LAYOUT_STRUCT for a memory-layout reason, and quietly giving them a table would meet the schema's needs while missing the point. |

### `IntWidth`

IntWidth names a concrete integer width, used where a target requires one and proto does not supply it.  FlatBuffers enums carry an explicit underlying type; proto enums are always varint-encoded int32. Defaulting every generated enum to `int` wastes three bytes per value in a struct, which is exactly where it is least affordable.

| Value | # | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `INT_WIDTH_UNSPECIFIED` | 0 | INT_WIDTH_UNSPECIFIED defaults to INT_WIDTH_INT32, matching proto's own encoding. |
| `INT_WIDTH_INT8` | 1 | INT_WIDTH_INT8 is a signed byte, -128 to 127. |
| `INT_WIDTH_UINT8` | 2 | INT_WIDTH_UINT8 is an unsigned byte, 0 to 255. The usual choice for a small closed enum in a high-rate message. |
| `INT_WIDTH_INT16` | 3 | INT_WIDTH_INT16 is a signed 16-bit integer. |
| `INT_WIDTH_UINT16` | 4 | INT_WIDTH_UINT16 is an unsigned 16-bit integer. |
| `INT_WIDTH_INT32` | 5 | INT_WIDTH_INT32 is a signed 32-bit integer, matching proto's own enum encoding. |
| `INT_WIDTH_UINT32` | 6 | INT_WIDTH_UINT32 is an unsigned 32-bit integer. |
| `INT_WIDTH_INT64` | 7 | INT_WIDTH_INT64 is a signed 64-bit integer. |
| `INT_WIDTH_UINT64` | 8 | INT_WIDTH_UINT64 is an unsigned 64-bit integer. Legal, and almost never what an enum needs. |
